lessons.title: Prototype Objects & [[Prototype]] Internal Links
lessons.description: Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object called its prototype — this is the foundation of inheritance.

sections.heading: What is a prototype?
paragraphs: A prototype is another object that your object can delegate property lookups to. When you access a property that doesn't exist on an object, JavaScript walks up the prototype chain until it finds it or reaches the end.
list: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link
If a property isn't found on the object, JavaScript looks at its prototype
This creates a chain: obj → obj.prototype → Object.prototype → null

codeExamples.heading: Prototype chain in action
explanation: Object.create(animal) creates a new object with animal as its prototype.
When rabbit.eats is accessed, it's not found on rabbit, so JavaScript looks at animal.
The chain continues until the property is found or the end is reached.
This is how JavaScript implements inheritance without classes.

practice.task: Create a base object with a method. Create two objects that inherit from it using Object.create. Call the method on each child object.
hints: Call child1.greet() — it works via the prototype chain.

keyTakeaways: Every object has an internal link to its prototype via [[Prototype]].
Property lookups walk up the prototype chain until found or null is reached.
Object.create() creates objects with a specified prototype.
This delegation mechanism is the foundation of JavaScript's inheritance model.
lessons.challenge: Map out the prototype chain of a plain object: {}. What links exist all the way to null?

lessons.title: Prototype Chain Property Lookups & Shadowing
lessons.description: When a property exists on both an object and its prototype, the object's own property takes priority.

sections.heading: Property shadowing
paragraphs: If you set a property on an object that already exists on its prototype, the new property is created directly on the object — 'shadowing' the prototype version.
list: Own properties always shadow prototype properties
The prototype property is not modified — it's just hidden
Use hasOwnProperty() to check if a property is truly on the object
Use in operator to check both the object and its prototype

codeExamples.heading: Shadowing and property checks
codeExamples.code:
let parent = { color: "red" };
let child = Object.create(parent);

console.log(child.color);  // "red" (from parent)

child.color = "blue";  // creates own property
console.log(child.color);  // "blue" (own property shadows parent)
console.log(parent.color); // "red" (parent unchanged)

console.log(child.hasOwnProperty("color"));  // true
console.log("color" in child);  // true
console.log("color" in parent);  // true
explanation: Before setting child.color, the lookup goes to the prototype.
After setting it, child has its own color property that shadows the prototype.
hasOwnProperty() returns true only for the object's own properties.
in checks the entire chain — own and inherited properties.

practice.task: Create a prototype chain where a child shadows a parent property. Use hasOwnProperty and the in operator to verify which properties are own vs inherited.
hints: Create a child via Object.create and set child.type = "pet".

keyTakeaways: Own properties always take priority over prototype properties.
Setting a property creates an own property that shadows the prototype.
hasOwnProperty() checks only the object's own properties.
in operator checks the entire prototype chain.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that recursively finds all inherited (non-own) properties of an object up the prototype chain.

lessons.title: Function .prototype vs Instance __proto__
lessons.description: Functions have a .prototype property for creating instances. Instances have a __proto__ link to that prototype.

sections.heading: Two different prototypes
paragraphs: There are two properties that confuse beginners: .prototype (on functions) and __proto__ (on instances). Understanding the difference is key.
list: func.prototype — an object that becomes the prototype of instances created with new
instance.__proto__ — the internal link to the prototype (same as func.prototype)
Use Object.getPrototypeOf() instead of __proto__ (it's the official way)
Every function has a .prototype, but only constructors use it with new

codeExamples.heading: prototype vs __proto__
explanation: Dog.prototype is the object that will become the prototype of all Dog instances.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf() instead of __proto__ — it's the official API.
Methods defined on .prototype are shared by all instances — efficient memory.

practice.task: Create a constructor function with a method on its prototype. Create 2 instances and verify they share the same prototype using Object.getPrototypeOf.

keyTakeaways: .prototype is on the function and becomes the prototype of new instances.
__proto__ is on instances and links to the function's prototype.
Methods on .prototype are shared by all instances — efficient and clean.
lessons.challenge: Create a Person constructor and a Student constructor that inherits from Person using Object.create(). Verify the full prototype chain.

lessons.title: Pure Prototypal Inheritance using Object.create()
lessons.description: Create inheritance relationships directly between objects without constructor functions.

sections.heading: Object.create() for inheritance
paragraphs: Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. This lets you build inheritance relationships directly between objects — no constructors needed.
list: Cleaner than constructor functions for simple inheritance
The pattern used by many modern frameworks

codeExamples.heading: Object.create() inheritance
explanation: The init method acts as a constructor for setting up instance data.
This is pure prototypal inheritance — objects inherit directly from other objects.

practice.task: Create a shape object with a describe() method. Create a circle and rectangle that inherit from it, each with their own area() method.

keyTakeaways: Object.create() creates objects with a specified prototype — clean inheritance.
Objects can inherit directly from other objects without constructors or classes.
This is the purest form of prototypal inheritance in JavaScript.
Method lookup walks the chain: instance → parent → grandparent → Object.prototype.
lessons.challenge: Build a 3-level prototype chain using Object.create() and verify property access and method calls at each level.
